deep.reconstruction:
Context: This page is a draft of Riemann's remarks for the public disputation tied to his Göttingen doctoral dissertation, 'Grundlagen für eine allgemeine Theorie der Functionen einer veränderlichen complexen Größe' (1851). The next page continues with themes from the dissertation: the surface S, mappings between plane and solid figures, and conformality conditions.

(1) Framing. Riemann says the dissertation was not written with a learned (polemical) aim. Because it is to supply the material for the disputation, he will single out points where 'men of recognised reputation' have asserted the opposite.

(2) First point: the concept of a function of a complex variable. In the dissertation, w is called a function of z = x+iy when dw/dz is independent of dz. Equivalently, the difference quotient has one limit whatever the direction of the increment, which amounts to the Cauchy–Riemann equations.
- Riemann distinguishes two opposing conceptions.
- The first grants functions this property but does not accept it as sufficient for a definition. Presumably this is the view that a function must be given by an analytic expression in x+iy.
- The second does not grant functions the property at all.

(3) The theorem on which the first view relies. For a function of a+b, written f(a+b):
  ∂/∂a f(a+b) = ∂/∂b f(a+b).
Riemann's justification, in modern form, for a, b and f real: one may speak of a derivative only if the ratio Δf / Δ(a+b) tends to a fixed limit as Δ(a+b) → 0. Since only the increment of the sum a+b enters, it is immaterial whether the increment is taken as an increment of a or of b. Both partial derivatives therefore equal f'(a+b).

(4) Implicit point (my completion, not written on the page). Put a = x and b = iy. The equality then reads ∂f/∂x = ∂f/∂(iy), i.e. ∂f/∂x = -i ∂f/∂y. These are the Cauchy–Riemann equations.
- The argument carries over only if the difference quotient has a direction-independent limit.
- That direction-independence is exactly the property Riemann takes as the definition.
- So the theorem is not a consequence of being 'an expression in a+b' that comes for free in the complex case. Its validity presupposes Riemann's defining property.
- The page breaks off before this conclusion is drawn.
errors: No mathematical error. The real-variable argument (both partials equal f'(a+b) by the chain rule / definition of derivative) is correct.
The page stops before stating explicitly why the argument fails or needs the direction-independence hypothesis for complex b = iy; the intended conclusion is reconstructed, not written.

results.what: d/da f(a+b) = d/db f(a+b), justified from the definition of the derivative (only the increment of a+b matters)
results.modern_name: Chain rule for f(a+b); in complex form the Cauchy–Riemann equations f_x = -i f_y
results.usually_credited_to: Cauchy–Riemann equations: d'Alembert, Euler, Cauchy (1814/1825); Riemann 1851 for their use as the definition of a complex function

results.what: Defining a complex function by direction-independence of the derivative, contrasted with definition by analytic expression
results.modern_name: Riemann's (geometric/differential) definition of holomorphic function vs. Weierstrassian/expression-based definition

deep.surprise_reason: This is a draft of disputation remarks defending the well-known definitional stance of Riemann's 1851 dissertation. It is historically interesting as evidence of his awareness of opposing views from established authorities, but it contains no new mathematics.

checkable.asserts: The partial derivatives of f(a+b) with respect to a and to b coincide.
For an analytic expression in x+iy, d/dx = d/d(iy), i.e. f_x = -i f_y (Cauchy–Riemann).
A function of x,y not depending on x+iy alone (complex conjugate) fails the condition, so the property is not automatic.

transcription_corrections: Line 1 likely reads 'Die Abhandlung ... nicht in gelehrter Absicht' (cf. the later full sentence), not 'gelehrter Zeitschrift'.
'Um diesen Satz [-Ansicht-] Auffassung' is more likely 'Von diesen beiden [-Ansicht-] Auffassungen über den Begriff einer Function ...'.
'ist also die erstere der einzigen in {+dieser+} [-so fern-] entgegengesetzt' should probably read 'ist also die erstere der meinigen in sofern entgegengesetzt, als sie die Eigenschaft ...'.
'die andere aber ferner der Art, daß' is likely 'die andere aber insofern, als sie diese Eigenschaft ihm überhaupt nicht beilegt'.
A folio/page number '51' appears in the right margin.
